source: Zhang, Cui, Chen, Wang, Zhang, Wang, Wu, Hu (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Five multi-agent debate (MAD) methods rarely beat plain chain of thought (CoT) and lose more clearly to self-consistency (SC) at similar calls or tokens. Full PDF text read.
numbers: 5 MAD methods x 9 benchmarks x 4 models (gpt-4o-mini, claude-3.5-haiku, Llama3.1 8B and 70B) = 36 settings; no MAD method won more than 20 percent of settings against CoT. gpt-4o-mini MMLU: CoT 80.73, SC 82.13, SoM 74.73, MultiPersona 75.47, EoT 67.87, ChatEval 79.13, AgentVerse 80.40. Budget set to 6 LLM calls; 3 repeats.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
limits: General knowledge, math and code; no clinical task. Gains came back when models were mixed (heterogeneity), so the result is about same-model debate.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 9 outside medicine: critic or debate loops should be compared with CoT-SC at equal calls; most do not win. Our S8 should be tested against sampling more first passes.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? (ICML)
finding: On medical question sets, several debate systems were roughly tied with self-consistency and Medprompt; debate was not clearly better. Medical sets favoured ensembling; non-medical sets favoured single agents. Full PDF text read.
numbers: Table 2, best setting per system (GPT-3.5 main runs): MedQA Medprompt 0.65, Society of Mind 0.64, Ensemble Refinement 0.64, ChatEval 0.60, SC 0.60, single agent 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58. PubMedQA Medprompt 0.77, single 0.75, SC 0.74, SoM 0.74. Text: on the medical sets every system except Multi-Persona beat the single agent; SC and Medprompt were top.
quote: multi-agent debating systems, in their current form, do not reliably outperform other proposed prompting strategies
limits: Differences of 0.01 to 0.05 with modest test sets; hyperparameter tuning mattered more than protocol. Cost was not equalised across systems, only reported.
agent_relevance: Medical evidence that a critic or debate structure is not the source of gains; sample-and-vote is a strong rival. Supports testing S8 against SC at equal cost (gap 9).

source: Wang, Jain, Zhang, Ray, Kumar, Athiwaratkun (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation
finding: When chain-of-thought SC gets the same budget (20 queries or 10k tokens), it beats Reflexion and multi-agent debate; Reflexion and debate can get worse with more budget. Full PDF text read.
numbers: Budget per question: max 20 queries or 10k tokens. MAD = 6 agents x 3 rounds = 18 queries. Reflexion = 10 proposals + 9 reflections = 19 queries. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, CSQA, HotpotQA. Reflexion with an oracle stop signal beat SC by a large margin; Reflexion with a GPT-4 evaluator did not beat Reflexion-SC, and the text says its evaluator was only slightly better than random guessing.
quote: certain strategies such as multi-agent debate or Reflexion can become worse if more compute budget is utilized
limits: No medical data. Reflexion needs a stop or success signal; with an oracle the loop works, with self-evaluation it does not.
agent_relevance: Strongest equal-budget evidence for gaps 1, 2 and 9: the reflection loop pays only if the trigger or judge is accurate. For our agent: sample more first passes before adding a reflection loop, and make the judge external where possible.

source: Wunderlich, Kaesberg, Wahle, Ruas, Gipp (2026) Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Counter-evidence to d01 and d03: with several models mixed (mixture of agents), multi-agent beats SC at comparable compute; self-refinement alone was worse than CoT. Full PDF text read.
numbers: MMLU-Pro, 34 configurations, over 100 evaluations. CoT 64.3; SC (10 samples) 68.7; debate (4 agents, 2 layers) 70.0; mixture-of-agents (5 models, 4 layers) 71.4. Self-refinement stayed below the CoT baseline. Gains by item difficulty (CoT solve rate over 20 runs, 1000 items): easy 94.4 base, +2.2; medium 53.0 base, +8.5; hard 8.4 base, +9.0 at 15-20x CoT compute.
limits: General benchmark; mixed-model setups are heterogeneous. Hard items are those with under 25 percent solve rate, so hard here is very hard.
agent_relevance: Self-refinement (the pure second look) lost; aggregation across different solvers won. The largest absolute gain sits on hard items, which supports a difficulty gate for spending extra passes (gap 3).

source: Tran, Kiela (2026) Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets
finding: At matched thinking-token budgets, one agent that reasons in one pass matches or beats sequential, debate, ensemble and role-based multi-agent setups on multi-hop questions. Full PDF text read.
numbers: Models: Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro. Data: FRAMES, MuSiQue 4-hop. Budgets 100, 500, 1000, 2000 thinking tokens. SAS best or statistically tied (bootstrap 95 percent CI) at every budget except 100 tokens. Example R1-70B FRAMES, one mid budget: SAS 0.448 vs Sequential 0.391 vs Debate 0.397. Multi-agent used more thinking tokens than SAS. Authors found API budget-control artifacts, especially in Gemini.
limits: Multi-hop retrieval QA, not diagnosis. Multi-agent became competitive when single-agent context use was degraded or compute was large.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 9 for QA and gap 6 in part: a reasoning model with an equal thinking budget already does what a critic pipeline does. Matched-token control must be in any test of our S5 and S8.

source: Tang, Zou, Zhang, Zhao, Zhang, Cohan, Gerstein (2024) MedAgents
finding: MedAgents (role-playing expert discussion) beat zero-shot CoT with 5-sample SC by about 1 to 4 points on average, not by large margins, and it costs many more calls. Full PDF text read, Table 2.
numbers: Average over 9 medical sets (300 items each). GPT-4: zero-shot 80.6, zero-shot CoT 80.8, zero-shot CoT+SC 83.0, few-shot CoT+SC 85.4, MedAgents 86.7. MedQA GPT-4: zero-shot CoT+SC 74.5 vs MedAgents 83.7. GPT-3.5: zero-shot CoT+SC 70.9, few-shot CoT+SC 71.6, MedAgents 72.1. Cost about 1.41 dollars per 100 questions, about 40 s per question. SC used 5 samples at temperature 0.7.
limits: Calls and tokens not equalised. Zero-shot CoT alone hurt GPT-3.5 (67.8 to 58.3). Few-shot CoT+SC is only 1.3 points under MedAgents for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 in medicine: the multi-agent gain over a voted single agent is small (GPT-4 +1.3 over few-shot CoT+SC) and not token-matched. A critic loop should not be credited with more than that until matched.

source: Kim, Park, Breazeal et al. (2024) MDAgents: adaptive collaboration of LLMs for medical decision-making
finding: An adaptive scheme that first rates case complexity and then picks solo or group handling beat a fixed solo CoT-SC with about 1.5x the API calls. Solo beat group on simple sets. Full PDF text read, Table 2 and section 4.4.
numbers: GPT-4, 3 seeds. CoT-SC vs MDAgents: MedQA 83.9 vs 88.7; PubMedQA 58.7 vs 75.0; DDXPlus 59.5 vs 77.9; SymCat 83.3 vs 93.1; JAMA 68.0 vs 70.9; MedBullets 76.0 vs 80.8. API calls: solo 5-shot CoT-SC 6.0; MedAgents group (N=5) 20.3; MDAgents adaptive (N=3) 9.3. Solo beat group on MedQA (83.9 vs best group 81.3).
limits: Calls not equal (9.3 vs 6.0) and tokens not reported as matched. High seed variance on some rows (for example PubMedQA CoT-SC +/-5.0).
agent_relevance: Closest medical support for a difficulty gate: routing by complexity beat both always-solo and always-group, with fewer calls than always-group. Supports gap 3 as a design idea, though not matched-token.

source: Huang et al. (2025) m1: Unleash the Potential of Test-Time Scaling for Medical Reasoning
finding: In medical QA, more thinking tokens help up to about 4K tokens, then flatten or drop. Forcing the model to keep thinking by appending Wait did not help and sometimes pushed correct answers to wrong ones. Full PDF text read.
numbers: Models m1-7B and m1-32B (fine-tuned on 1K to 23K traces). Optimal reasoning budget about 4K tokens, beyond which accuracy saturates or declines (overthinking). Budget forcing: minimal improvement. A failure case shows a first correct answer turned wrong after forced re-think because faulty knowledge was retrieved.
quote: Budget forcing ... helps models double-check answers but does not necessarily improve the overall medical QA performance
limits: Authors' own tuned models, medical MCQ; budget-forcing curves are in figures and exact per-step numbers were not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Direct medical test of a forced second look at the reasoning-model level (gap 6): the extra pass adds errors when knowledge is wrong. Fits the human result that the second look needs content knowledge.

source: Bi, Chen, Song et al. (2025) Exploring Efficiency Frontiers of Thinking Budget in Medical Reasoning
finding: Across 15 medical datasets, accuracy rises roughly with the log of the thinking budget: fast gains up to about 256 tokens, small gains after 512. Small models gain most from thinking. Full PDF text read.
numbers: Qwen3 1.7B to 235B and DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B to 70B; budgets 0, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 and unlimited. Thinking gave +15 to 20 percent for small models and +5 to 10 percent for large. Attending-level sets 70 to 88.5 percent; chief-level sets 59.5 to 80 percent. Qwen3-235B 62.5 vs 1.7B 45 on chief cardiovascular. Unconstrained traces 168 to over 15,000 tokens.
limits: Budgets are truncations of the model's own thinking, not separate second passes. Quality of the dataset labelling and judge not audited here.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: reasoning models already spend tokens on internal re-checking, and gains flatten early. An added scaffold pass should be tested at equal total thinking tokens; the headroom above 512 tokens is small on routine items.

source: Moell, Aronsson, Akbar (2025) Medical Reasoning in LLMs: An In-Depth Analysis of DeepSeek R1
finding: R1 answered 93 of 100 MedQA cases; the seven errors showed anchoring, trouble with conflicting data, too few alternative diagnoses and overthinking. Wrong answers had longer reasoning. Full PDF text read.
numbers: N=100 MedQA cases, 93 percent correct. Reasoning length: wrong answers mean 8,118 characters vs right 3,648; Welch t=-2.74, p=0.032 (with only 7 wrong). Authors suggest under 5,000 characters as a rough sign of reliability.
limits: Only 7 errors; p=0.032 is fragile; length may reflect difficulty not error. Single model, single dataset.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model still anchors and fails to widen the differential, so a second-look prompt is not clearly redundant (gap 6). Reasoning length may serve as a cheap difficulty signal for gating (gaps 3 and 8).

source: Liu, Chen, Li, Qi et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (COLM)
finding: Self-reflection (aha) words already appear in base models, and in R1-Zero they are not linked to higher accuracy. Full PDF text read, section 2.3.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3-Base-685B produced self-reflection keywords on the 500 MATH questions with the R1 template; in R1-Zero such behaviour was more frequent but not positively correlated with higher accuracy (their Sec. F).
quote: these behaviors are not positively correlated with higher accuracy
limits: Keyword counting, math only. Measures the appearance of reflection words, not whether the reflection changed an answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: reflection-style text in reasoning models is not proof that a real second look happens. A scaffold step must be judged by answer flips, not by reflection words.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Self-Correction Blind Spot (COLM 2026)
finding: Models fix an error when it is shown as coming from the user but not when it is the same error in their own earlier output. Appending Wait removes most of the gap. Full PDF text read.
numbers: 14 non-reasoning open models: average blind spot 64.5 percent. Mean accuracy internal-error baseline vs external vs Wait: SCLI5 0.499 vs 0.910 vs 0.957; GSM8K-SC 0.183 vs 0.881 vs 0.796; PRM800K-SC 0.200 vs 0.620 vs 0.504. Wait cuts the blind spot by 89.3 percent; 5,306 correction traces cut it by 76.0 percent.
limits: Injected errors in math and logic tasks, not medical; not the model's free choice of what to check.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 6: the second look works if the prompt re-frames the earlier text as someone else's claim (a colleague proposed) or opens with Wait. Design hint for S8: present the first answer as external. Untested in diagnosis.

source: Kumar, Zhuang, Agarwal et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Gives the first full flip table for a model asked to revise its own answer. The untrained base model turned many right answers wrong. Full PDF text read, Tables 1 and 2.
numbers: Gemini 1.0 Pro, MATH, second attempt. Base model: accuracy 52.6 to 41.4 (-11.2); wrong-to-right 4.6 percent of items, right-to-wrong 15.8 percent. Self-Refine 52.8 to 51.8 (right-to-wrong 4.2, wrong-to-right 3.2). Trained SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4 (+4.4; wrong-to-right 5.8, right-to-wrong 1.4).
limits: Math, one model family, results need training; the numbers show the size of harm and benefit, not what a prompt-only agent gets.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: net flip rate of an untreated second look can be strongly negative (about 3.4 harmful flips per helpful one). Our agent must log both flip directions and keep a revision only when it is justified.

source: Liu, Nassereldine, Yang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Have Intrinsic Self-Correction Ability
finding: Reconciles the pro and con papers: the wording of the second-look prompt and the sampling temperature decide the sign. A prompt that presumes an error (find problems with your answer) damages accuracy; a neutral prompt leaves accuracy about unchanged or slightly up. Full PDF text read, Table 2.
numbers: CommonsenseQA before vs after: GPT-4 84.11 vs prompt set 1 (presumes problems) 66.34, set 2 72.56, set 3 (fair) 84.60; GPT-3.5 75.92 vs 76.00 (fair); Llama3.1 75.18 vs 73.55 / 82.80 / 75.27. HotpotQA GPT-3.5 31.0 to 47.0 (fair prompt). The authors assume that under a fair prompt the model changes almost nothing.
limits: The fair-prompt gain is small on CommonsenseQA (+0.08 to +0.67) and rests on the model rarely changing; no medical task; zero temperature required.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the framing of the S8 prompt is a hidden variable. Use a neutral check question, not find your mistake. This matches the human finding that plain be-careful instructions add nothing.

source: Zhang, Chen, Pan et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is right, is well calibrated, and can stop reasoning early; the model does not use this itself. Full PDF text read.
numbers: Reasoning models (R1-Distill family) on math and logic. In-distribution probes ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1; some over 0.9 on AIME. Using the probe to exit early cut inference tokens by 24 percent with no loss.
limits: Needs white-box access; not medical; different task from diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: correctness signals exist inside the model but verbal confidence is a poor gate (see d18). For an API-only agent, use sample agreement instead.

source: Chen, Cai, Ji et al. (2024) HuatuoGPT-o1: Towards Medical Complex Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Teaching a model long reasoning with backtracking, new paths, verification and correction raised medical MCQ accuracy over plain answers and short CoT. Full PDF text read.
numbers: LLaMA-3.1-8B ablation (MedQA / MedMCQA / PubMedQA / MMLU-Pro med / GPQA med): SFT on answers only 65.2 / 58.1 / 75.4 / 58.5 / 48.7; simple CoT 66.6 / 59.2 / 75.4 / 57.0 / 46.7; complex CoT 69.0 / 57.9 / 77.7 / 59.4 / 51.0 (paper states complex CoT adds an average of 4.3 points; baseline for that average not rechecked); plus PPO with a verifier 72.6 / 60.4 / 79.2 / 63.1 / 57.5. Complex CoT averaged 712 tokens.
limits: Training-based and verifier-rewarded, so not a prompt-only scaffold; complex CoT is also longer, so token count is confounded with reflection.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: reflection-style traces help when trained in with an answer verifier. Supports the point that the verifier, not the wording, carries the gain.

source: Samsel, Dharma, Rezaei et al. (2026) Too agreeable to be accurate? Sycophancy and diagnostic instability of LLMs (Artif Intell Med)
finding: When told Are you sure?, LLMs changed diagnoses and the net effect was harmful: far more correct answers became wrong than the reverse. Abstract only (full text not reached).
numbers: 120 vignettes (40 MultiCaRe case narratives, 80 MedMCQA-derived), 10 LLMs, 4 prompt conditions, 3 runs x 2 passes = 28,800 responses. Neutral baseline accuracy 51.8 percent fell to 42.2 percent after Are you sure? (flip rate 32.8 percent). Correct-to-incorrect 544 vs incorrect-to-correct 198. GPT-5 74.4 to 75.3; Claude Sonnet 4 flip rate 58.6 percent and -36.4 points.
limits: LLM-as-judge scoring; vignette sets; a pushback prompt differs from a self-initiated second look. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Closes much of gap 3 for diagnosis: an unstructured challenge gives a net flip ratio of about 2.7 harmful to 1 helpful, strongly model-dependent. Our S8 needs a guard that keeps the first answer unless new evidence appears.

source: Savage, Wang, Gallo et al. (2025) Large language model uncertainty proxies: discrimination and calibration for medical diagnosis and treatment (JAMIA)
finding: For diagnosis tasks, sample agreement predicts correctness better than token probability or verbalized confidence, which is over-confident. Abstract only.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2, Llama3 on 3 open-ended patient-scenario sets. Sample consistency by sentence embedding ROC AUC 0.68 to 0.79 (poor calibration); by GPT annotation AUC 0.66 to 0.74 (accurate calibration). Verbalized confidence consistently overestimated.
limits: AUC in the 0.66 to 0.79 range is moderate; abstract only; older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: use disagreement across independent first passes to decide when to run S8, not the model's stated confidence. Moderate power, so use it as a soft gate.

source: Sibbald, de Bruin, van Merrienboer (2013) Checklists improve experts' diagnostic decisions (Med Educ)
finding: A checklist used in a verification step after the expert's own reading corrected errors without raising cognitive load. Independent Toronto and Maastricht group. Abstract read.
numbers: 15 ECG experts, 18 ECGs, 4 conditions. Errors corrected per ECG: 0.29 +/- 0.77 with checklist vs 0.03 +/- 0.61 without (p<.01). Net errors per ECG across conditions: 0.39 vs 1.04 (p<.01). Cognitive load 3.7 vs 3.3 (n.s.). Checklist cost more time and longer interpretations (p<.01).
limits: Small N (15), ECG reading rather than reasoning from history, within-subject. Checklist content was supplied by the researchers.
agent_relevance: Gaps 10 and 5: an independent result that a structured verification pass after the first read helps experts. Fits S8 placed after S5. The content of the checklist matters (see K09).

source: Sibbald, de Bruin (2012) Feasibility of self-reflection as a tool to balance clinical reasoning strategies (Adv Health Sci Educ)
finding: Residents knew whether they had read an ECG fast or analytically, but being told to switch strategy on re-reading did not help; being told to be analytic helped. Abstract read.
numbers: Exp 1: 6 residents, 8 ECGs, self-rated strategy vs expert rating rho=0.69 (p<.0001); analytic readers took 40 percent longer. Exp 2: 24 residents re-read 8 ECGs; balancing vs potentiating instruction F(1,188)=0.22, p=0.64; analytic instruction F(1,188)=15, p<.0001.
limits: Small N; ECGs only; instruction to be analytic is a different manipulation from for-and-against listing.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 (independent group): second reading with an analytic instruction raised scores, but customised strategy-switch instructions did not. Supports a fixed analytic second look over adaptive switch-mode prompts.

source: Sibbald, Monteiro, Sherbino, LoGiudice, Friedman, Norman (2022) Should electronic differential diagnosis support be used early or late? (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Giving an electronic list of alternative diagnoses either early or late raised the chance that the correct diagnosis was in the differential by about the same amount. Abstract read.
numbers: 67 students, 62 residents, 61 practising physicians; 16 written cases; randomised early vs late. Early use added 2.32 diagnoses (CI 2.10-2.49); late use added 0.89 (CI 0.69-1.10). Correct diagnosis present in differential +7 percent (early) and +8 percent (late), both p<.001.
limits: Outcome is correct diagnosis being present in the list, not final accuracy; written cases; commercial tool.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: independent test of order. Alternatives supplied late worked as well as early for getting the right answer into the list, so strict bottom-up generation is not required for the benefit of a broader differential. Useful for S5 (widen) after S4. It does not test the DR claim directly.

source: Lambe, O'Reilly, Kelly, Curristan (2016) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Twenty-eight studies; guided reflection was the most consistently successful intervention (five studies); samples mostly early-career doctors. Abstract read.
numbers: 28 studies in five categories: educational, checklists, cognitive forcing, guided reflection, instructions at test. Heterogeneous measures. Review judged results promising but not ready for firm policy.
limits: Review written before Staal 2022; pooled effect not calculated; author overlap with the Mamede network cannot be excluded for the guided-reflection studies.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10: no patient-outcome trial in the pool; evidence base is training-level and vignette-level. Counts against over-claiming for any real-practice benefit.

source: Ludolph, Schulz (2018) Debiasing Health-Related Judgments and Decision Making: A Systematic Review (Med Decis Making)
finding: Most debiasing studies in health reported at least partial success, but only 13 of 87 studies targeted health professionals, and transfer to real settings was flagged as the main gap. Abstract read.
numbers: 68 articles / 87 studies from 2,748 abstracts; 60 interventions at least partly successful; 36 cognitive strategies (for example consider-the-opposite) and 33 technological; 13 aimed at professionals, 74 at the general population; quality score 26.2 to 92.9 percent (mean 68.7).
limits: Counts at least partially successful, which is a lenient bar; mostly lay participants.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: confirms that clinician and real-practice evidence for reflection-style debiasing is thin. Consider-the-opposite is the most tested strategy, which matches the against step in our S8.

source: Mamede, Zandbergen, de Carvalho-Filho et al. (2024) Role of knowledge and reasoning processes as predictors of susceptibility to anchoring bias (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Residents with more knowledge of discriminating features resisted anchoring more; slower, less confident diagnosis (a sign of analytic effort) did not by itself protect. Same lab as the deliberate-reflection studies. Abstract read.
numbers: 68 internal medicine residents, two phases a week apart; 6 cases with and without salient distracting features. Higher-knowledge group fell for anchoring less often on SDF+ cases (p=0.02). Time and confidence differed between SDF+ and SDF- cases (p<.001, p=0.02) but did not differ between knowledge groups (p=0.88, p=0.96).
limits: Same research network (not independent); knowledge groups split by test score, so correlational; N=68.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: again points to retrieved contrast knowledge, not process effort, as the thing that resists anchoring. No LLM test found of a retrieved discriminating-features aid versus a process prompt, so gap 7 stays open.

source: Chamberland, Setrakian, St-Onge, Bergeron, Mamede, Schmidt (2019) Does providing the correct diagnosis as feedback after self-explanation improve diagnostic performance? (BMC Med Educ)
finding: A Canadian site (with Mamede and Schmidt as co-authors): self-explanation plus feedback helped near-transfer cases one week later, not far-transfer. Abstract read.
numbers: 94 third-year students, 3 arms. Near-transfer accuracy: immediate feedback 90.73 (SD 10.69), delayed feedback 89.92 (13.85), no feedback 82.03 (17.66), p<.05. Far transfer: no difference.
limits: Not independent of the Rotterdam lab; the feedback manipulation is not the second look itself.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a second site with an overlapping author group reproduces a delayed, near-transfer benefit. Still no fully independent replication of the delayed-learning effect found.

source: Miao, Wen, Luo, Li (2026) MedARC (Int J Med Inform); Sun et al. (2026) Model confrontation and collaboration (Cell Rep Med)
finding: Two 2026 medical debate frameworks report gains over zero-shot and CoT baselines, without a token-matched self-consistency baseline in the abstracts. Abstracts read.
numbers: MedARC: PubMedQA yes/no 72.9 (zero-shot) to 77.2 with DeepSeek-V3 as backbone. MCC: MedQA 92.6 percent, PubMedQA 84.8 percent, top-1 diagnosis 80 percent in diagnostic dialogue; MCC outperformed all single models it used.
limits: Abstracts only; baselines named are zero-shot and CoT, so the gain over SC at equal compute is unknown. MCC mixes diverse models, which d01 and d04 show is the part that helps.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the medical debate gains remain unmatched. They are consistent with d01 and d04 that model diversity, not critique, may be the driver.

source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning (Acad Med)
finding: Telling residents to be slow and thorough did not raise accuracy compared with telling them to be fast. Independent McMaster/Ottawa/McGill group. Abstract read. (Already used for K03; added here as the independent-site anchor for gap 10.)
numbers: 204 second-year residents (96 speed in 2010, 108 reflect in 2011), 20 internal medicine cases. Accuracy 44.5 vs 45.0 percent (n.s.); time 69 vs 89 s per case (P<.001); wrong cases took 17 s longer.
limits: Cohorts run in different years, not randomised in parallel; instruction only, no structured second look.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: independent failure of the cheap slow-down version while the structured version is supported in the Mamede lab. Keep S8 structured, not an exhortation.
